content:
If you have COPD as well as arthritis, breathlessness and sore joints can feed each other: you do less because walking is hard on your chest and your knees, your muscles weaken, and everything then feels harder. Moving regularly at a pace that leaves you slightly out of breath but still able to talk is safe and helps both conditions. Ask your GP or COPD nurse about pulmonary rehabilitation, tell the team about your arthritis so exercises can be adapted, and ask your pharmacist to check your inhaler technique if your hands are stiff. Get urgent help for breathlessness that is much worse than usual, chest pain or blue lips. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is for people living with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) and any kind of arthritis, and the people who help them. If you have a cough, fever or phlegm that has changed colour right now, start with chest infections and arthritis. If tiredness rather than breathlessness is the main problem, see RA fatigue in later life.

Why lungs and joints make each other harder

COPD and arthritis are both common in later life, and many people have both. Each one can make the other feel worse:

  • Painful knees, hips or feet make walking slower and more effortful, so you get out of breath sooner.
  • Being breathless makes you avoid walking, stairs and exercise, so the muscles that protect your joints get weaker.
  • Weaker legs make getting out of a chair, climbing stairs and walking outside harder still, and can make falls more likely.
  • Courses of steroid tablets for COPD flare-ups can, over time, affect bones and muscles. Your GP may talk to you about bone protection.

The good news is that the same thing helps both: regular, steady movement that you build up slowly.

Being breathless when you move is not harmful

Feeling a bit out of breath when you are active is normal with COPD and is not damaging your lungs. A useful guide is to move at a pace where you are breathing harder but can still talk in short sentences. If you cannot speak at all, slow down or stop and recover, then carry on more gently.

The same is true of joint pain. Some aching during and after exercise is common with arthritis and usually settles within a day. If pain is much worse the next day, do a little less next time rather than stopping altogether.

Pulmonary rehabilitation: ask for it

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a programme of exercise and education for people with lung conditions such as COPD. The NHS says programmes usually involve two or more group sessions a week for at least six weeks, run by physiotherapists, nurses and other professionals. It can help you do more before you get out of breath and improve your confidence. NICE recommends it for people with COPD who are limited by breathlessness.

  • Ask your GP, practice nurse or COPD nurse to refer you. In some areas you can refer yourself.
  • Tell the team about your arthritis before you start: which joints, what makes them worse, and whether you use a stick or frame. Exercises can be done seated or adapted, for example cycling instead of walking, or smaller step-ups.
  • If getting there is the problem, ask about transport, home-based programmes or online sessions.
  • If you were offered a place before and could not go because of your joints, it is fine to ask again.

Everyday movement that helps both

  • Little and often. Several short walks around the house or garden spread through the day are easier on both chest and joints than one long walk.
  • Sit-to-stands. Standing up from a firm chair a few times, using your hands if you need to, is one of the most useful exercises for leg strength.
  • Seated exercise on bad days: knee straightening, ankle pumps and arm raises while sitting. See seated exercise for flare days and good days.
  • Breathe out on the effort. Breathe out as you stand up, lift or climb a step. Pursed-lip breathing (breathing out slowly through lips shaped as if you are whistling) can help you recover.
  • Use a walking aid if it helps. A rollator with a seat lets you stop and rest anywhere, and leaning forward slightly on it can ease breathlessness. A physiotherapist can check that a stick or frame is the right height. See choosing mobility aids.
  • Plan the day. Do harder tasks when your breathing and joints are usually at their best, and sit down for jobs such as washing, dressing and preparing food.

Inhalers when your hands are stiff

Arthritis in the hands, wrists or shoulders can make it hard to press, twist or hold an inhaler, and poor technique means less medicine reaches your lungs.

  • Ask your pharmacist or practice nurse to watch you use your inhaler. They can check your technique at an appointment or a medicines review.
  • Ask whether a spacer, an inhaler aid that makes the canister easier to press, or a different type of inhaler would suit your hands better. Only your prescriber can change the inhaler, but the pharmacist can suggest it.
  • Keep inhalers somewhere easy to reach, not in a high cupboard or a bag across the room.

Arthritis medicines and your lungs

  • Methotrexate can rarely cause inflammation of the lungs. The NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 immediately if you get a persistent cough, chest pain, difficulty breathing or new breathlessness while taking it. Tell your rheumatology team that you have COPD.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis itself can sometimes cause inflammation in the lungs. New or worsening breathlessness should always be checked, not put down to your COPD or age.
  • Anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen are not right for everyone. Check with a pharmacist before using them, especially if you have heart, kidney or stomach problems.
  • DMARDs, biologics and steroids can make chest infections more likely or harder to spot. See methotrexate in later life for what to watch for.

Protect your chest through the year

  • Have your yearly flu vaccine and ask about the pneumococcal vaccine and any other vaccines you are eligible for. If you take medicines that affect your immune system, tell the person giving the vaccine.
  • If you smoke, stopping is the most important thing you can do for COPD. Free NHS stop smoking services can help.
  • Keep your home warm in winter; cold air can make breathing and joint stiffness worse. See keeping warm and moving in a cold home.
  • Ask your GP or COPD nurse for a written COPD self-management plan, so you know what to do if your symptoms change.

When to get help

  • Call 999 if you are struggling to breathe much more than usual and cannot speak in sentences, have chest pain, your lips or skin turn blue or grey, or you are suddenly confused or very drowsy.
  • Contact your GP, COPD nurse or NHS 111 the same day if you are more breathless than usual, coughing more, your phlegm has changed colour, or you have a high temperature, especially if you take methotrexate, other DMARDs, biologics or steroids.
  • Seek urgent advice for a single hot, swollen, very painful joint with a temperature.
  • See your GP if breathlessness or joint pain is slowly stopping you doing everyday things, or you have had a fall.

For family and carers

Encourage short bouts of activity rather than doing everything for the person. Walk alongside at their pace, leave time to stop and rest, and help them get to pulmonary rehabilitation if transport is a barrier.

Common questions

Can I do pulmonary rehabilitation if my knees or hips are bad?

Usually, yes. The team can adapt exercises for arthritis, for example by using seated exercises or a static bike. Tell them about your joints at the first assessment.

Should I rest when I am breathless and my joints ache?

Rest to recover your breath, then carry on gently. Long spells of sitting usually make both COPD and arthritis harder over time.

Is my breathlessness from COPD or something else?

Breathlessness can have many causes, including heart problems, anaemia and, rarely, side effects of arthritis medicines. If it is new, worse or different from usual, tell your GP.
